content.title: Research Methodology Consultation
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and her psychology professor.
content.script:
Emma: Professor Miller, do you have a minute to look at my survey design?
Professor Miller: Sure, Emma. Did you narrow down your topic on sleep and memory?
Emma: Yes, I want to compare exam scores between freshmen and seniors.
Professor Miller: Relying only on self-reported sleep logs can be pretty inaccurate, though.
Emma: Oh, I hadn't thought about students guessing their sleep hours.
Professor Miller: Why not pair the questionnaire with data from wearable fitness trackers?
Emma: That's a great idea, and the wellness center lends them out.
Professor Miller: Exactly. Update your ethics form first, and I'll sign it tomorrow.

questions.q: Why does the professor say this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Professor Miller: Relying only on self-reported sleep logs can be pretty inaccurate, though.
options: To warn that students often estimate their own sleep hours inaccurately on logs.
To point out that freshmen and seniors take completely different types of exams.
To explain that the psychology department has already funded a similar study.
To suggest that wearable fitness trackers are too expensive for undergraduate projects.
questions.why: Professor Miller says this to point out the methodological flaw of relying solely on self-reported sleep logs, since students often guess their sleep hours.

questions.q: What will the student most likely do next?
options: Cancel her study and choose a new psychology topic.
Revise her ethics approval form to include wearable tracker data.
Begin distributing paper questionnaires in the freshmen dormitories.
Purchase fitness trackers from an off-campus electronics store.
questions.why: At the end of the conversation, the professor instructs Emma to update her ethics form first so he can sign it tomorrow.

content.title: Library Reserve & Interlibrary Loan
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university librarian.
content.script:
Lucas: Excuse me, I'm looking for Dr. Chen's textbook on medieval architecture.
Ms. Rivera: Let me check our catalog. Both print copies are currently checked out.
Lucas: Oh no, my seminar summary is due this Wednesday morning.
Ms. Rivera: Professor Chen actually placed a copy at the course reserve desk.
Lucas: Great! Can I borrow it overnight to read at my apartment?
Ms. Rivera: Reserve books stay in the library for three-hour loans only.
Lucas: That's fine. Which chapter covers Gothic cathedral vaults?
Ms. Rivera: You can check the table of contents right over at Desk Two.

questions.q: What does the librarian imply when she says this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Ms. Rivera: Reserve books stay in the library for three-hour loans only.
options: The textbook is missing several pages from the chapter on Gothic cathedrals.
The book is only available to graduate students in architecture.
The student cannot take the reserve copy home overnight to his apartment.
The student must submit an interlibrary loan form to read the book.
questions.why: By stating that reserve books stay in the library for three-hour loans only, Ms. Rivera implies Lucas cannot borrow it overnight.

questions.q: Why does the student urgently need the textbook?
options: He needs to photocopy the bibliography for Professor Chen.
He lost the copy he borrowed earlier in the semester.
He is preparing slides for a guest lecture on Friday.
He has to complete a seminar summary due on Wednesday morning.
questions.why: Lucas mentions that his seminar summary is due this Wednesday morning.

content.title: Coral Reef Bleaching Office Hours
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and her marine biology professor.
content.script:
Maya: Dr. Vance, could you clarify something from today's lecture on coral bleaching?
Dr. Vance: Of course, Maya. Which part was unclear?
Maya: When ocean temperatures rise, why do corals expel their symbiotic algae?
Dr. Vance: Heat stress damages the algae's photosynthesis, causing them to release toxic oxygen molecules.
Maya: So the coral ejects the algae to protect its own tissue?
Dr. Vance: Exactly, though losing the algae also deprives the coral of its main food source.
Maya: Does that mean bleached coral dies immediately?
Dr. Vance: Not right away. If water cools quickly, corals can absorb new algae and recover.

questions.q: According to the professor, why does a coral expel its symbiotic algae during heat stress?
options: Because the heat-damaged algae begin producing toxic oxygen molecules.
To make room for cold-water bacteria in its skeleton.
To attract predatory fish that clean the reef surface.
Because the algae consume too much calcium carbonate.
questions.why: Dr. Vance explains that heat stress damages the algae's photosynthetic process, causing them to release toxic oxygen molecules that threaten the coral's tissue.

questions.q: What does the professor imply when he says this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Dr. Vance: Not right away. If water cools quickly, corals can absorb new algae and recover.
options: Bleached corals are already dead and cannot be restored.
Coral bleaching is reversible if ocean temperatures drop in time.
Corals no longer require sunlight once they turn white.
Bleaching only occurs in shallow freshwater lakes.
questions.why: Dr. Vance implies that coral bleaching is not immediately fatal and can be reversed if water temperatures cool quickly.

content.title: Dormitory Heating Maintenance Request
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a campus housing coordinator.
content.script:
Daniel: Hi, Ms. O'Connor. The radiator in my dorm room stopped working last night.
Ms. O'Connor: Which residence hall and room number are you in, Daniel?
Daniel: Oak Hall, Room 304, on the third floor.
Ms. O'Connor: Does the radiator make a clanging sound, or is it completely cold?
Daniel: It's completely cold, even when I turn the valve all the way.
Ms. O'Connor: That usually means air is trapped inside the steam pipe.
Daniel: Do I need to stay in my room for the technician?
Ms. O'Connor: No, just sign this entry waiver and they'll fix it before four.

questions.q: Why does the housing coordinator say this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Ms. O'Connor: That usually means air is trapped inside the steam pipe.
options: To explain that the main boiler in Oak Hall has been turned off for the season.
To scold the student for leaving the window above the radiator open overnight.
To provide a likely diagnosis for why the student's radiator is completely cold.
To suggest that the thermostat on the third floor needs new batteries.
questions.why: Ms. O'Connor says this to explain the probable technical cause of the cold radiator based on Daniel's description.

questions.q: What must the student do before leaving the housing office?
options: Pay a maintenance fee for the replacement valve.
Wait in his dorm room until four o'clock.
Borrow a portable space heater from the front desk.
Sign an entry waiver allowing the technician into his room.
questions.why: Ms. O'Connor tells Daniel that he does not need to stay in his room if he signs the entry waiver.

content.title: Renaissance Art History Paper Topic
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and her art history professor.
content.script:
Hannah: Professor Lindqvist, I'd like to write my term paper on fifteenth-century Italian frescoes.
Professor Lindqvist: That's a fascinating period, Hannah, but it's far too broad for ten pages.
Hannah: What if I focus on how painters prepared mineral pigments in Florence?
Professor Lindqvist: Better, especially if you examine how trade with Venice changed their color palette.
Hannah: Like ultramarine blue imported from Afghanistan?
Professor Lindqvist: Precisely. Comparing ultramarine in two Florentine altarpieces would make a sharp argument.
Hannah: Where can I find chemical analyses of those specific paintings?
Professor Lindqvist: Check the museum conservation bulletins in our digital art archive.

questions.q: Why does the professor say this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Professor Lindqvist: That's a fascinating period, Hannah, but it's far too broad for ten pages.
options: To encourage her to narrow the scope of her research paper topic.
To inform her that fifteenth-century frescoes are not covered in the course syllabus.
To warn her that there are no translated sources on Italian frescoes in the library.
To let her know another student in the seminar already selected the same topic.
questions.why: Professor Lindqvist says this to guide Hannah toward narrowing her overly broad topic so it fits a ten-page term paper.

questions.q: What source does the professor recommend the student consult?
options: Merchant shipping logs at the municipal courthouse.
Museum conservation bulletins in the digital art archive.
An introductory textbook on medieval oil painting.
Audio recordings from last semester's guest lecture.
questions.why: At the end of the conversation, Professor Lindqvist recommends checking the museum conservation bulletins in the digital art archive.

content.title: Academic Internship Resume Review
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university career advisor.
content.script:
Alex: Thanks for looking over my resume before Friday's environmental engineering career fair.
Career Coach Brenda: Happy to help, Alex. Why is your hydrology lab project buried at the bottom?
Alex: Because it was an unpaid course project rather than a paid job.
Career Coach Brenda: Engineering recruiters care much more about technical skills than whether you were paid.
Alex: Should I move it above my summer job at the campus bookstore?
Career Coach Brenda: Definitely, and mention the water-quality software you used to model runoff.
Alex: I used GIS mapping tools to analyze fifteen local stream samples.
Career Coach Brenda: Put that exact number in your first bullet point before printing copies.

questions.q: Why does the career advisor ask this question?
questions.audioExcerpt: Career Coach Brenda: Happy to help, Alex. Why is your hydrology lab project buried at the bottom?
options: To ask if he received a low grade on the final lab report.
To check whether he has finished analyzing the fifteen stream samples.
To point out that his relevant technical project should be featured more prominently.
To suggest that he remove the hydrology project from his resume.
questions.why: Career Coach Brenda asks why the hydrology project is buried at the bottom to prompt Alex to move his most relevant engineering experience higher up.

questions.q: What does the career advisor suggest the student include in his project description?
options: The names of the other students in his lab group.
A letter of reference from his bookstore manager.
A list of all introductory courses he took during freshman year.
Specific details about the GIS software and number of stream samples analyzed.
questions.why: Career Coach Brenda advises him to mention the water-quality/GIS software and include the exact number of stream samples (fifteen) in his first bullet point.

content.title: Dining Hall Meal Plan Adjustment
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a campus dining services coordinator.
content.script:
Chloe: Hi, I'd like to switch from the unlimited meal plan to the ten-meal plan.
Mr. Grant: Sure, Chloe. Have you found that you aren't using all your dining hall swipes?
Chloe: Yeah, I have morning biology labs, so I usually make breakfast in my suite.
Mr. Grant: Good timing—tomorrow is actually the final day to downgrade plans without a fee.
Chloe: Will the difference in cost be refunded to my bank account?
Mr. Grant: It goes onto your student ID card as Campus Flex Dollars.
Chloe: Can I spend Flex Dollars at the coffee cart in the science building?
Mr. Grant: Yes, at any campus café or the university market.

questions.q: Why does the student want to reduce her campus meal plan?
options: She eats breakfast in her suite before her morning biology labs.
The main dining hall is too far from her dormitory.
She is moving off campus at the end of the month.
The dining hall stopped serving vegetarian options.
questions.why: Chloe explains that because of her morning biology labs, she usually prepares breakfast in her suite and does not use all her swipes.

questions.q: What does the coordinator imply when he says this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Mr. Grant: Good timing—tomorrow is actually the final day to downgrade plans without a fee.
options: The dining hall will close permanently after tomorrow.
The student will be charged a penalty fee if she waits until next week to switch.
Students are not allowed to change meal plans during the autumn semester.
The difference in cost will be mailed to her parents as a paper check.
questions.why: By noting that tomorrow is the final day to downgrade without a fee, Mr. Grant implies that waiting longer would incur a fee.

content.title: Environmental Science Field Sampling Schedule
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and his environmental science professor.
content.script:
Noah: Dr. Patel, my lab partner just dropped the course, and Saturday's wetland trip is coming up.
Dr. Patel: Thanks for letting me know, Noah. Soil core sampling definitely requires two people.
Noah: Should I join one of the other pairs in our Friday lab section?
Dr. Patel: Three people per coring tube gets crowded on the narrow boardwalk.
Noah: Is there anyone else working solo right now?
Dr. Patel: Actually, Priya from the Tuesday section also needs a partner for Saturday.
Noah: Can we collect data together even though we're in different lab sections?
Dr. Patel: Yes, share the raw measurements, then write your lab reports independently.

questions.q: Why does the professor say this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Dr. Patel: Three people per coring tube gets crowded on the narrow boardwalk.
options: To apologize for not having enough protective boots for three students.
To warn that all of the other pairs have already completed their wetland sampling.
To explain why she does not want the student to join an existing pair.
To remind him that university rules prohibit groups larger than two in lectures.
questions.why: Dr. Patel says this to explain the practical reason why Noah should not join an existing two-person group on the narrow wetland boardwalk.

questions.q: What does the professor allow Noah and Priya to do?
options: Submit a single joint lab report for both sections.
Postpone their wetland trip until the following weekend.
Analyze archived soil samples in the indoor lab instead.
Collect soil measurements together and write separate reports.
questions.why: Dr. Patel tells Noah that he and Priya can collect and share the raw measurements on Saturday and then write their lab reports independently.

content.title: Campus Theater Lighting Crew Sign-Up
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and the campus theater stage manager.
content.script:
Sofia: Hi, Mr. Brooks. Are you still looking for volunteers for the autumn play?
Mr. Brooks: We sure are, Sofia. Our costume crew is full, but we need lighting assistants.
Sofia: I've never operated a theater lighting board before, though.
Mr. Brooks: That's completely fine—we run a hands-on training workshop this Thursday evening.
Sofia: What would I be doing during the actual performances?
Mr. Brooks: You'd program cue transitions on the console from the control booth.
Sofia: That sounds fun! Do I need to attend every rehearsal?
Mr. Brooks: Only the final dress rehearsals during tech week in November.

questions.q: What does the stage manager imply when he says this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Mr. Brooks: That's completely fine—we run a hands-on training workshop this Thursday evening.
options: Prior experience is not required to volunteer for the lighting crew.
Only theater majors are permitted to operate the lighting console.
Volunteers must purchase their own toolkits before Thursday.
Assistants must attend every rehearsal starting this week.
questions.why: When Sofia mentions she has never operated a lighting board, Mr. Brooks reassures her that it is fine because training is provided.

questions.q: When will the student be required to attend rehearsals?
options: Every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon throughout the semester.
During the final dress rehearsals in tech week in November.
Only on opening night of the autumn play.
Every weekend morning starting in October.
questions.why: Mr. Brooks specifies that she only needs to attend the final dress rehearsals during tech week in November.

content.title: Economics Seminar Presentation Schedule
content.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and his economics professor.
content.script:
Ethan: Professor Chen, would it be possible to move my seminar presentation from next Tuesday?
Professor Chen: Next Tuesday is our unit on central bank interest rates, Ethan. What's the conflict?
Ethan: Our debate team qualified for the regional tournament, and we travel Monday night.
Professor Chen: Congratulations! However, your presentation topic is tied directly to Tuesday's reading.
Ethan: What if I switch topics and present on microfinance in Week Eight instead?
Professor Chen: Rachel is scheduled for Week Eight, unless she agrees to swap dates with you.
Ethan: I spoke with Rachel before class, and she's ready to present on Tuesday.
Professor Chen: In that case, email me confirmation from both of you by five o'clock.

questions.q: Why does the professor say this?
questions.audioExcerpt: Professor Chen: Congratulations! However, your presentation topic is tied directly to Tuesday's reading.
options: To explain that the syllabus prohibits missing class for extracurricular events.
To point out that there are no remaining class sessions left in the semester.
To explain why simply moving his current presentation topic to another week is problematic.
To remind him that he has already rescheduled his presentation once before.
questions.why: Professor Chen says this to explain why Ethan cannot simply present his central bank topic on a different date.

questions.q: How is the scheduling conflict resolved?
options: Ethan will record a video of his presentation before leaving on Monday.
The debate tournament was moved to the following weekend.
Professor Chen will lecture on central bank rates in Ethan's place.
Ethan will swap presentation dates and topics with his classmate Rachel.
questions.why: Ethan explains that he spoke with Rachel, who agreed to swap dates and present on Tuesday while he presents on microfinance in Week Eight.
